source_read: PDF, pp. 159-175 (all pages; Table 2 across pp. 162-166 and Tables 1, 3 and 4 checked, with pp. 172-173 rendered at 110 dpi). Step 1 (blind extraction) not run this round, per the round brief.

design.note: The editor asked whether this is a systematic review (AMSTAR 2, as in the sc_lappin_2017 precedent) or a narrative review. I agree with AI reader 24: systematic review without meta-analysis. The paper reports its databases, its 46 search terms, the months of searching, explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria applied to all 59 records found, the resulting count of 33, a pre-defined extraction list and a structured extraction of every included study in Table 2. That is a documented systematic search with explicit selection, which is what separates the two categories; the missing protocol, duplicate screening and appraisal are failures AMSTAR 2 scores as unmet items rather than reasons to reclassify. The authors' own label, 'a critical review' (title), is a self-description, and the editors' narrative-review checklist (METHODS 5.3) would have nowhere to put the search and the extraction table. Practically nothing turns on the choice: critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2 and high risk under the narrative checklist both mean the review is cited for pointers and for which tasks have and have not shown differences, never for an effect size.

key_findings.note: Checked the abstract (p. 159) and the Method, Identification of Studies (1st paragraph begins p. 160 and continues p. 161; 2nd paragraph p. 161): 59 found, 33 included, searches July to September 2008 in PsycINFO and Medline, peer-reviewed English-language reports, a minimum time since last use, and the abstract's statement that all but one study was cross-sectional. The 46 search terms are 40 task pairings plus 6 others, as the card's design detail says.

Checked p. 161, 1st paragraph of the updating section: 9 studies, all but one by combinations of the authors, 7 with computation span deficits, 2.48 span items (2.75 vs 5.23), 27 of the 44 in one study also in another.
Checked p. 167, 2nd paragraph of the updating section: the ANCOVA results, the exclusion-based re-analysis (amphetamine, cocaine, poppers) and the inconsistent correlations are all there.

Checked the 5th and 6th paragraphs of the updating section (the 6th begins p. 167 and continues p. 168): 'fairly robust', the 400-tablet abstinent group, the inconsistent correlations and the two tasks where controlling for cannabis left no deficit.

Checked p. 168: 6 studies, the plus/minus and number/letter nulls, the matched-group Wisconsin studies, the study in which polydrug controls did worse, the 11 heavier-use participants in a region with limited exposure to other drugs, and the summary sentence.

Checked pp. 168-170: 17 studies, 8 Stroop studies with 6 nulls, the two equivocal ones including the Hong Kong sample of 100 people who had used no other illicit drugs, the unreplicated random letter generation finding with 10 current and 10 former users, and the summary sentence.
Checked p. 170: three Chicago word fluency studies with 27 of 104 participants shared, three FAS studies with deficits and three without, and the summary sentence calling the results contradictory.

Checked pp. 170-172 and Tables 3 and 4 (p. 171): 18 studies, 11 in Table 3 and 12 in Table 4, two studies with deficits in people abstinent at least 6 months, lifetime means of 149.69 (96.91) and 169 (252), and the executive-demand reading.
Checked p. 172, Discussion 1st paragraph; the four conclusions are in those terms.

Checked the Discussion 3rd paragraph (begins p. 172, continues p. 173): one genuinely prospective study, all others cross-sectional or quasi-experimental, pre-existing differences cannot be ruled out, and both arguments the card reports.

Checked p. 173, Discussion 4th paragraph: cannabis present in every ecstasy group except the Hong Kong study, the ANCOVA shared-variance argument, and the statement that failure of homogeneity of regression makes ANCOVA results invalid.
Checked p. 173, Discussion 6th paragraph: laboratory tasks as proxies, and the self-report limitation on everyday-functioning evidence.

reporting_issues.note: Confirmed: the Discussion (p. 173) says the mean estimated consumption in Schilt et al. was 3.2 tablets 'after 3 years'; the source gives a mean of 11.1 months between sessions in the ecstasy group within a 3-year recruitment window (Schilt et al., 2007, p. 731, which I read for the other card).
Confirmed: the overlaps are stated (27 of 44 on p. 161; 27 of 104 on p. 170) and the studies are still counted individually in the task-by-task tallies and in Tables 3 and 4.

overall.note: Critically low confidence; four unmet critical items. The reasoning's restriction, that the review may be cited for which tasks have and have not shown differences and for the fact that only one included study was prospective, is what the paper supports.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. The conclusions track the vote counts, and the review states its own limits, including that controlling for cannabis removed deficits on two updating tasks and that the correlational data are inconsistent. 'Fairly robust' (p. 167) is the one phrase that runs ahead of evidence drawn mostly from the authors' own overlapping samples, and the card says so.

missed: Scope: the review covers tasks empirically mapped onto updating, shifting, inhibition and access to long-term memory, plus visuospatial memory, and explicitly excludes other executive tasks (p. 173). Verbal list-learning tests, the measures that carry the verbal-memory literature and the Ung meta-analysis, are not in it. The card's cannot_establish should say so, because the review is otherwise easy to cite for 'memory' in general.

Table 2 is the comparison source for the Wareing entries that Ung et al. (2026) appear to have transcribed wrongly (sample sizes and lifetime tablets of the 2004 verbal and visuospatial papers swapped against their labels; 591.33 here against 291.33 there). The card should carry a pointer, since the editor will otherwise have the finding on only one of the two cards.

The study credited with the one Wisconsin deficit and with spatial-span deficits in Table 3 is Halpern et al. (2004), the authors' pilot (11 heavier-use participants, more than 50 episodes), not the 2011 study in this batch. The 2011 study (sc_halpern_2011) is the authors' own larger attempt at that pilot, and it did not reproduce the spatial-span or Wisconsin differences. Any use of Murphy's tally needs that noted.

The Hong Kong study the review describes (100 people who had used ecstasy and no other illicit drugs, with regular alcohol and tobacco use excluded, no significant difference after correction for multiple comparisons) is a second minimal-polydrug sample alongside Halpern et al. (2011). It is second-hand here, but it belongs in the replication field of this card and is relevant to cl_mdma_minimal_polydrug, which currently speaks of a single such study.

Table 4 lists Schilt et al. among the studies with no visuospatial deficit (judgement of line orientation from memory), which independently matches Schilt's own null for that test. Worth recording as a consistency check between the two cards.
